F.note: High voltages can electrocute; high currents can overheat wiring and start fires.

q.text: What is the main risk from high currents?
q.why: High current heats conductors.

I.note: Large or high-voltage capacitors can hold a dangerous charge after switch-off. Discharge them before working on equipment. Bleeder resistors across them provide a leakage path.

q.text: Why must large capacitors be discharged before you work on a power supply?
choices: They can hold a dangerous charge after switch-off
q.why: Stored charge can give a severe shock.

Full.note: Lethal voltages may exist in equipment, and live circuits are exposed as soon as the case is removed.

q.text: When can lethal voltages become accessible in equipment?
choices: As soon as the case is removed
q.why: The case is the protection.

F.note: Never remove a safety earth. Earthing needs special care: consult a competent professional (an electrician) before changing earthing arrangements.

q.text: Who should you consult before changing your station's earthing?
q.why: Earthing errors can be dangerous.

Full.note: With Protective Multiple Earthing (PME), the consumer's main earth terminal is connected to the supply neutral. Under severe fault conditions this can put dangerous voltages on earthed metalwork, including a separately earthed radio station, risking fatal shock or fire. Follow the RSGB guidance and get professional advice before connecting an RF earth in a PME property.

q.text: Why is extra care needed with RF earths in a property with PME?
choices: Faults can raise the earth to a dangerous voltage
q.why: The earth is tied to neutral, which can rise under fault conditions.

F.note: In a UK 3-pin plug: brown is live (to the fuse), blue is neutral, green-and-yellow is earth (top pin). The cord grip must hold the outer sheath.

q.text: In a UK mains plug, which wire goes to the fuse?
q.why: The fuse is in the live.

F.note: Fit fuses as the manufacturer says. A fuse is a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit when too much current flows. If one blows, find out why before replacing it.

q.text: A fuse blows. What should you do?
choices: Find the cause before replacing it
q.why: The fuse blew for a reason.

I.note: Fuses may be quick-blow or slow-blow (anti-surge) to cope with an initial surge; fit the type specified. Rate it correctly: without other guidance, just above the normal working current.

q.text: Equipment draws 2.5 A. Which fuse is most suitable without other guidance?
q.why: Just above normal current.

F.note: An RCBO (residual current breaker with overcurrent protection) gives far better protection against electric shock than a fuse, which only protects against excess current. The RCBO trips if it detects current leaking to earth, such as through a person.

q.text: Why does an RCBO protect better against shock than a fuse?
choices: It detects small currents leaking to earth
q.why: An RCBO trips on an imbalance between live and neutral.

F.note: Only work inside equipment with the power disconnected, and follow the manufacturer's servicing instructions.

q.text: What should you do before opening a transceiver to work inside?
q.why: Work only on unpowered equipment.

I.note: Only work on live equipment if there's no practical alternative and you fully understand the risks and precautions.

q.text: When is it acceptable to work on live equipment?
choices: Only if it's impractical otherwise and the risks are understood
q.why: Live work is a last resort.

Full.note: Don't work on live equipment unless it isn't practicable to do otherwise, and take suitable precautions against shock (for example, one hand only, insulated tools, someone else present).

q.text: Which is a sensible precaution if live work can't be avoided?
choices: Keep one hand away and use insulated tools
q.why: Reduce the chance of current crossing your body.

F.note: Control all equipment from a clearly marked master switch that others know about. In an electrical accident or fire, first switch off the power. Don't touch the casualty until they're clear of the supply; then call for help. Never use water on an electrical fire.

q.text: Someone has an electric shock in your shack. What do you do first?
choices: Pull them away by the hand
q.why: Cut the supply first so you don't become a casualty too.

F.note: Some batteries can supply very high currents, dangerous if short-circuited. Charge them as the manufacturer says. Lithium batteries in particular can catch fire or explode if damaged or charged wrongly. Fuse the battery lead close to the battery.

q.text: Which battery type is particularly prone to fire if mistreated?
q.why: Lithium cells can go into thermal runaway.

I.note: Vehicle batteries supply very high currents that can start fires, and their acid is corrosive. Charging gives off explosive hydrogen, so ventilate well.

q.text: Why must lead-acid batteries be charged in a well-ventilated place?
choices: They need cooling air for the charger
q.why: Hydrogen gas can explode.

F.note: Wear eye protection when using tools, to stop metal particles (swarf) damaging your eyes.

q.text: Why should you wear goggles when drilling metal?
q.why: Flying metal particles can damage eyes.

F.note: All tools, including power tools, can be dangerous: handle them with care and take sensible precautions.

q.text: Which tools need careful handling?
q.why: Any tool can cause injury.

I.note: Take care with screwdrivers, drills, saws and files. Keep your fingers behind the blade.

q.text: Where should your fingers be when using a craft knife?
q.why: So a slip doesn't cut you.

I.note: Hold anything being drilled, sawn or filed securely in a vice or clamp so it can't slip or spin.

q.text: Why clamp a metal box before drilling it?
choices: To stop it spinning or slipping
q.why: A spinning workpiece can injure.

I.note: Always remove chuck keys and locking keys before switching on a power tool, or they can be thrown out at high speed.

q.text: What must you do before starting a drill?
q.why: A key left in can be flung out.

I.note: Mark a hole with a centre punch first, to stop the drill bit wandering.

q.text: Why use a centre punch before drilling?
q.why: The dimple guides the bit.

I.note: A bench-mounted pillar drill is safer than a hand-held one: it's steadier, the work can be clamped to the table, and the drill can't twist out of your hands.

q.text: Why is a pillar drill safer than a hand drill?
choices: It's steady and the work can be clamped
q.why: Better control and support.

F.note: Wear eye protection when soldering, as solder and flux can spit. Keep the iron in its stand when not in use. Work in a well-ventilated area to avoid breathing flux fumes. Some solders contain lead, so wash your hands afterwards.

q.text: Why should a soldering area be well ventilated?
q.why: Flux fumes are harmful.

F.note: Putting up antennas can be dangerous; have someone to help you. At least one adult should be present.

q.text: Why should you have help when putting up an antenna?
q.why: Someone can assist and raise the alarm.

F.note: Use a ladder at the correct angle: 4 up for every 1 out. Secure it so it can't slip, and don't overreach.

q.text: A ladder reaches 8 m up a wall. How far from the wall should its foot be?

F.note: Use a tool belt when working at height, to stop tools falling. Wear a hard hat when working at height or when others are working above you.

q.text: Who should wear a hard hat during antenna work?
choices: Only the person on the ladder
q.why: Falling objects endanger people below.

F.note: The main health effect of RF exposure is heating of body tissue. The eyes are particularly vulnerable.

q.text: What is the main health effect of exposure to strong RF?
q.why: RF energy is absorbed as heat.

I.note: At 100 W, especially with a high-gain antenna, the EMF compliance distance can be several metres. When mobile, pedestrians may be within it; if they are, especially when you're stationary, stop transmitting.

q.text: You're parked transmitting at 100 W and someone walks right up to your mobile antenna. What should you do?
q.why: They may be inside the compliance distance.

Full.note: ICNIRP publishes guidance on exposure to RF fields. Don't exceed the recommended levels, especially where the public have access.

q.text: Which body publishes guidance on RF exposure?
q.why: The International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection.

F.note: Guidance on safe RF levels is available from government and international bodies: the UK Health Security Agency and ICNIRP.

q.text: Which UK body gives guidance on RF exposure?
q.why: UKHSA (with ICNIRP).

F.note: A waveguide is a metal tube carrying microwaves. Never look into one, or stand in front of a high-gain antenna, as it may be in use.

q.text: Why should you never look down a microwave waveguide?
choices: It may be carrying power that can damage your eyes
q.why: Eyes are particularly vulnerable to RF heating.

F.note: Don't touch antennas or other conductors carrying RF while transmitting: they can cause painful burns. Mount antennas where people can't touch them by accident. (Low-power handhelds are an exception.)

q.text: Why should antennas be mounted out of reach?
choices: Touching them while transmitting can cause RF burns
q.why: RF on the element can burn.

F.note: Very high antennas may need lightning protection. The local authority's building control department may be able to advise.

q.text: Who may be able to advise on lightning protection for a tall mast?
q.why: Building control can advise.

I.note: Gas-discharge arrestors, spark gaps and bleed resistors give limited protection against static build-up on antennas. They won't survive a direct strike.

q.text: What does a gas-discharge arrestor protect against?
q.why: Limited protection from static charge only.

Full.note: Thunderclouds carry heavy static charges, which can ionise the air into a low-resistance path to ground: lightning. A strike endangers people, buildings and equipment. Disconnect and earth antennas when storms approach.

q.text: What should you do with your antennas when a thunderstorm approaches?
choices: Disconnect them from the equipment and earth them
q.why: Reduces the risk to you and the equipment.

F.note: Site and secure masts, wires and antennas properly. Never put them near overhead power lines: contact, or arcing from a line, can kill.

q.text: Why must antennas never be put near overhead power lines?
choices: Contact or arcing can be fatal
q.why: Power lines carry lethal voltages.

F.note: Don't leave cables trailing across the floor: they're trip hazards and their insulation can fray.

q.text: Why avoid cables across the floor?
choices: They're trip hazards and insulation can fray
q.why: Safety, not looks.

F.note: Excessive volume in headphones can damage your hearing.

q.text: What risk comes from loud headphones?
q.why: Prolonged loud audio damages hearing.

F.note: Operating outdoors or in temporary premises brings new hazards: temporary mains connections, trailing cables, damp ground. Do a risk assessment, route cables safely and use RCD protection.

q.text: Which is a sensible precaution when operating portable outdoors?
choices: A risk assessment and RCD protection on mains
Using indoor extension leads on wet ground
q.why: Outdoor sites have extra electrical and trip hazards.

I.note: Hazards include overhead power lines, inadequate supplies, trailing cables, damp ground and high field strengths. Do a site survey and risk assessment, keep antennas away from the public and power lines, and use RCDs.

q.text: What should you do first when setting up a field station?
choices: Survey the site and assess the risks
q.why: Identify hazards before starting.

F.note: Safety is everyone's job. Watch for anything unsafe, warn others and report it, in your own shack and with visitors too.

q.text: You spot a frayed mains lead at a club meeting. What should you do?
q.why: Safety is everyone's responsibility.

Full.note: Operating mobile or maritime mobile brings hazards: insecure equipment, long or flexible antennas, accidental shorts to earth, and distraction from driving. Secure everything and don't let radio distract you.

q.text: Which is a hazard particular to mobile operation?
choices: Overhead power lines in the shack
q.why: Driving safely comes first.

Full.note: Carry out a risk assessment whenever an activity could harm you or others: identify the hazards, judge how likely and how severe harm would be, and decide how to reduce the risk.

q.text: What does a risk assessment consider?
choices: How likely harm is and how severe it would be
q.why: Likelihood and severity determine the precautions.

Full.note: Generators bring risks: earthing must be correct; fuel must be stored safely away from the generator; never refuel while it's running or hot; keep it in the open because of the exhaust fumes.

q.text: When should a generator be refuelled?
q.why: Fuel on hot parts can ignite.
